- graphify: Use for any question about a codebase, its architecture, file relationships, or project content — especially when graphify-out/ exists, where the question should be treated as a graphify query first. Turns any input (code, docs, papers, images, videos) into a persistent knowledge graph with god nodes, community detection, and query/path/explain tools.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

input.description: Find background workers started by server
input.prompt:
In this repository (/bench/home/work), I need to know exactly what background workers/runners/schedulers the server process actually STARTS at boot/startup, and what drives each one's scheduling (e.g., cron expression, setInterval, message queue consumer, DB polling loop, etc).

Please investigate:
1. Find the main server entrypoint(s) (look for things like server.ts/js, index.ts, app startup files, main.go, etc.)
2. Find where background jobs/workers/cron/schedulers are registered or started — search for terms like "cron", "setInterval", "setTimeout", "worker", "scheduler", "queue", "job", "runner", "BullMQ", "agenda", "node-cron", "background", "poll".
3. For each one that is actually wired up and started by the server (not just defined but never invoked), identify what triggers its execution (cron expression, interval duration, event, queue subscription, etc.) and cite the file path and line number.
4. IMPORTANT: Also check if there is any scheduling infrastructure present in the codebase (e.g. a cron library, job queue system, scheduler class) that is defined/imported but NOT actually used/started by the server — i.e. dead or unused scheduling infrastructure. Note this explicitly.

Report back with a list of "runner name — trigger mechanism — file:line" entries, and a separate note about any unused scheduling infrastructure. Be precise and cite exact file paths and line numbers. Do not guess — if something is ambiguous, say so.

## Summary

This is a Go codebase (usememos/memos). The server entrypoint is `cmd/memos/main.go`, which builds a `store.Store` and a `server.Server` and calls `s.Start(ctx)`. All background-runner wiring happens in `server/server.go`.

### Runners actually started at boot

**1. S3 presign runner — `time.Ticker`, 12-hour interval**
- Started from: `/bench/home/work/server/server.go:153-174` (`startBackgroundRunners`, called from `Start()` at line 129)
- Constructed/kicked off once immediately, then looped:
  - `s3presignRunner := s3presign.NewRunner(s.Store)` — `/bench/home/work/server/server.go:162`
  - `s3presignRunner.RunOnce(ctx)` (immediate first run) — `/bench/home/work/server/server.go:163`
  - `go func() { s3presignRunner.Run(s3Context) }()` (continuous loop) — `/bench/home/work/server/server.go:166-171`
- Actual trigger mechanism: `time.NewTicker(runnerInterval)` where `runnerInterval = time.Hour * 12` — `/bench/home/work/server/runner/s3presign/runner.go:27,30` (`Run` loop at lines 29-41). On each tick it calls `RunOnce` → `CheckAndPresign`, which batches through S3-stored attachments and refreshes presigned URLs that are within 4 days of their 5-day expiry.
- Given its own cancellable context (`s3Context`/`s3Cancel`) so it can be stopped independently on shutdown — `/bench/home/work/server/server.go:156-159`, stopped via `stopBackgroundRunners()` at line 176.

**2. In-memory cache cleanup loops (instance-setting/user/user-setting caches) — `time.Ticker`, 5-minute interval**
- Not called a "runner" in the code, but it is a genuine background loop spun up at process boot as a side effect of store construction, so worth listing:
- Started from: `store.New()` — `/bench/home/work/store/store.go:38-61`, called from `cmd/memos/main.go:64` (`storeInstance := store.New(dbDriver, instanceProfile)`), which runs before the HTTP server starts.
- Three caches are constructed (`instanceSettingCache`, `userCache`, `userSettingCache`), each via `cache.New(cacheConfig)` — `/bench/home/work/store/store.go:51-53`, with `CleanupInterval: 5 * time.Minute` — `/bench/home/work/store/store.go:42`.
- Each `cache.New()` call spawns its own goroutine: `go c.cleanupLoop()` — `/bench/home/work/store/cache/cache.go:83`, which runs `ticker := time.NewTicker(c.config.CleanupInterval)` and evicts expired items on each tick — `/bench/home/work/store/cache/cache.go:200-215`. So there are effectively 3 independent 5-minute cleanup goroutines running concurrently.

### Not a boot-time background worker (per-request goroutines, for completeness/exclusion)
These use `go func()` but are fired per HTTP request/event, not scheduled at startup, so they don't belong in the "runner" list:
- `internal/email/email.go:18` — async send inside an email-send call.
- `internal/webhook/webhook.go:44` — async dispatch inside a webhook-trigger call.
- `server/auth/authenticator.go:180` — async "last used" timestamp update per authenticated request.
- `server/router/api/v1/sse_handler.go:64` — `time.NewTicker` heartbeat, but this is created per SSE client connection, not once at server boot.

## Unused / dead scheduling infrastructure

**`internal/scheduler` package is a complete, unused cron scheduler.** It implements a "GitHub Actions-inspired cron job scheduler" (per its own doc comment) with standard 5/6-field cron expression parsing, timezone support, a middleware chain (logging/metrics/recovery), and graceful shutdown — files: `/bench/home/work/internal/scheduler/scheduler.go`, `job.go`, `parser.go`, `middleware.go`, `doc.go`.

I verified with `grep -rln "internal/scheduler"` across the whole repo: the **only** files that import it are its own test/example files:
- `/bench/home/work/internal/scheduler/example_test.go`
- `/bench/home/work/internal/scheduler/integration_test.go`

No file under `cmd/`, `server/`, or `store/` imports `internal/scheduler`. It is never registered with, or started by, `server.Server` or `cmd/memos/main.go`. This is dead scheduling infrastructure — fully built but not wired into the running server.

**`server/runner/memopayload.Runner` is also unused as a background runner.** It defines a `Runner` type with `NewRunner(store, markdownService)` and a `RunOnce(ctx)` method that batch-rebuilds the payload of *all* memos (`/bench/home/work/server/runner/memopayload/runner.go:14-72`). Grepping for `memopayload` usage across the repo shows `NewRunner` is never called anywhere outside its own file. The only production usage of this package is the standalone helper function `memopayload.RebuildMemoPayload(...)`, called synchronously inline during single-memo create/update request handling in `/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/memo_service.go:108` and `:447` — i.e., it runs as part of a normal API request, not as a scheduled/background job. So the `Runner`/`RunOnce` batch-rebuild machinery in that package is defined but never invoked as a background worker.

No cron/queue libraries (e.g., `node-cron`, BullMQ, agenda, asynq) appear in `go.mod`; `internal/scheduler` is a hand-rolled, dependency-free implementation, confirming it's bespoke unused infrastructure rather than a wrapper around an external system.
